title: Kojo and the Forest of a Thousand Lives

pages.text: Early morning mist curled through the tall trees of Kakum National Park in Ghana’s Central Region. Nine-year-old Kojo walked beside his aunt, Ranger Akosua, clutching his green notebook. ‘Auntie Akosua,’ he asked, ‘why do we protect all these wild bushes and insects when only the big trees give us shade?’
sentences: Early morning mist curled through the tall trees of Kakum National Park in Ghana’s Central Region.
Nine-year-old Kojo walked beside his aunt, Ranger Akosua, clutching his green notebook.
‘Auntie Akosua,’ he asked, ‘why do we protect all these wild bushes and insects when only the big trees give us shade?’
pages.alt: Kojo walks along a misty rainforest trail in Kakum National Park beside Ranger Akosua.

pages.text: Ranger Akosua paused beside a giant odum tree whose trunk rose like a pillar toward the sky. ‘A forest is not just a collection of big trees, Kojo,’ she said. ‘It is a community of habitats, the natural homes where thousands of living things shelter, feed and help one another survive.’

‘A forest is not just a collection of big trees, Kojo,’ she said.
‘It is a community of habitats, the natural homes where thousands of living things shelter, feed and help one another survive.’
pages.alt: Ranger Akosua touches the buttress roots of a giant odum tree while Kojo looks up at its high canopy.

pages.text: At the edge of the park, they passed Papa Kwesi’s shady cocoa farm. Tiny pale flowers grew right on the trunk of a cocoa tree. ‘Look closely,’ whispered Ranger Akosua. ‘Tiny flies called midges visit those flowers. As they drink nectar, they carry pollen from flower to flower. Without pollination by those tiny insects, no cocoa pods would grow!’

As they drink nectar, they carry pollen from flower to flower.
Without pollination by those tiny insects, no cocoa pods would grow!’
pages.alt: Kojo and Ranger Akosua look closely at tiny white cocoa flowers on a cocoa tree trunk near Papa Kwesi.

pages.text: Higher up on the canopy walkway, sunlight sparkled on millions of green leaves. ‘Every food web in the forest starts here,’ said Ranger Akosua. ‘Green plants are producers. They use sunlight, water and air to make their own food, and they release the oxygen we breathe.’
sentences: Higher up on the canopy walkway, sunlight sparkled on millions of green leaves.
‘Every food web in the forest starts here,’ said Ranger Akosua.
‘Green plants are producers.
They use sunlight, water and air to make their own food, and they release the oxygen we breathe.’
pages.alt: Kojo and Ranger Akosua stand safely on the Kakum canopy rope walkway among sunlit green treetops.

pages.text: Suddenly, the branches rustled! A troop of Diana monkeys with white throat fur leaped across the boughs, munching wild figs, while a yellow-casqued hornbill glided past. ‘And at dusk,’ said Ranger Akosua, ‘straw-coloured fruit bats fly out to eat fruit and drop seeds far and wide, planting new forest trees.’
sentences: Suddenly, the branches rustled!
A troop of Diana monkeys with white throat fur leaped across the boughs, munching wild figs, while a yellow-casqued hornbill glided past.

pages.alt: Diana monkeys eat figs in the canopy branches while a hornbill flies pastKojo and Ranger Akosua.

pages.text: ‘What about predators?’ asked Kojo. Ranger Akosua pointed to a green tree frog resting on a broad leaf and a crowned eagle circling high above. ‘Frogs eat beetles and flies, snakes and birds hunt frogs, and eagles hunt in the treetops. All these overlapping food chains join together into a food web.’

Ranger Akosua pointed to a green tree frog resting on a broad leaf and a crowned eagle circling high above.
‘Frogs eat beetles and flies, snakes and birds hunt frogs, and eagles hunt in the treetops.
All these overlapping food chains join together into a food web.’
pages.alt: A green rainforest frog sits on a wide leaf in the foreground while a crowned eagle circles high above the canopy.

pages.text: Back down on the cool, shaded forest floor, Kojo stepped over a fallen wawa log covered in bracket fungi, millipedes and busy termites. ‘Why doesn’t the forest floor pile up to the sky with dead leaves and old branches?’ he wondered aloud.
sentences: Back down on the cool, shaded forest floor, Kojo stepped over a fallen wawa log covered in bracket fungi, millipedes and busy termites.
‘Why doesn’t the forest floor pile up to the sky with dead leaves and old branches?’ he wondered aloud.
pages.alt: On the shaded forest floor, Kojo kneels beside a mossy fallen log covered with cream bracket mushrooms and a millipede.

pages.text: ‘Because of the decomposers!’ said Ranger Akosua, kneeling beside the log. ‘Fungi, termites, millipedes and tiny bacteria break down dead leaves and wood. Decomposition turns dead matter back into rich nutrients in the soil, feeding the roots of young saplings.’

‘Fungi, termites, millipedes and tiny bacteria break down dead leaves and wood.
Decomposition turns dead matter back into rich nutrients in the soil, feeding the roots of young saplings.’
pages.alt: Ranger Akosua points to tiny green seedlings sprouting from rich dark soil beside the decomposing log.

pages.text: By a clear forest stream, Ranger Akosua showed Kojo deep, round footprints in the mud made by a forest elephant. ‘When people cut down too many trees or pollute streams, the balance breaks,’ she said softly. ‘Animals lose their habitats, soil washes away, and even the cocoa farms lose their pollinators and rain.’

‘When people cut down too many trees or pollute streams, the balance breaks,’ she said softly.
‘Animals lose their habitats, soil washes away, and even the cocoa farms lose their pollinators and rain.’
pages.alt: Beside a clear forest stream, Kojo and Ranger Akosua examine large round elephant footprints in the soft mud.

pages.text: Kojo drew a circle in his green notebook: sunlight to leaves, insects to flowers, bats to seeds, and fungi back to the soil. ‘Nothing in the forest lives alone,’ he said. ‘Protecting the big trees means protecting the smallest midges and mushrooms too.’ Ranger Akosua smiled. ‘Now you think like a ranger.’ The end.

activities.definition: Natural homes where plants and animals find shelter, food and water.
distractors: baskets used to carry cocoa beans

activities.question: How do tiny midges help Papa Kwesi’s cocoa trees?
options: They carry pollen between cocoa flowers so cocoa pods can grow
They eat the tough shells of ripe cocoa pods
They chop down dead branches in the night
activities.explanation: Midges pollinate the small cocoa flowers; without pollination, the trees cannot produce cocoa pods.

activities.question: Why are green plants called producers in a food web?
options: They use sunlight, water and air to make their own food
They hunt insects in the dark
They only grow on top of rocks
activities.explanation: Green plants produce food using energy from sunlight through photosynthesis.

activities.question: What job do decomposers like fungi, termites and bacteria do on the forest floor?
options: They break down dead leaves and wood into rich nutrients for the soil
They block sunlight from reaching the canopy
activities.explanation: Decomposers recycle dead plant and animal material back into soil nutrients that feed new plants.

activities.prompt: What would happen to farms and streams near a forest if all the trees and insects disappeared?
Put these steps of the forest nutrient cycle in order.
items: Green leaves use sunlight to grow high in the canopy.
Animals eat fruits and drop seeds across the forest.
Old leaves and branches fall to the forest floor.
Fungi and termites break down the dead wood into rich soil for new saplings.

activities.prompt: What is one living thing near your school or home that you can help protect?

glossary.definition: The natural homes where plants and animals live and grow.
Moving pollen from one flower to another so seeds and fruit can form.
Green plants that make their own food using sunlight, water and air.
Animals that hunt and eat other animals for food.
Living things like fungi, termites and bacteria that break down dead matter.
Nourishing substances in soil or food that help living things grow.
